plot_extraction.response_text:
A high school senior remembers his father’s animated Anansi stories while struggling with the man’s sudden disappearance. His father leaves for Ghana, promising to return in two weeks, but remains out of contact for months, leaving the teenager to help support his sick mother and younger sister while their family faces financial hardship.

Working long shifts unloading trucks at a home improvement store, the narrator finds camaraderie with Cato, a former track star whose injury derailed his future, and Reese, an older coworker who encourages the narrator to attend college. Despite several acceptances, the narrator fears he must abandon his plans and remain at the store to support his family.

These experiences are interwoven with his father’s tale of Anansi outwitting Lion to save three rabbit children. The story echoes the narrator’s feelings about his unreliable father and his own forced responsibility. One week before graduation, the father unexpectedly appears at the store, three and a half months late. Though the narrator feels anger, pride, relief, and gratitude, he cannot express them. When his father offers him a ride home, he simply accepts.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story uses a first-person retrospective voice that remains closely aligned with the narrator’s adolescent consciousness. The narration is observant, wry, and emotionally restrained: pain is rarely declared outright and instead emerges through practical details, private fantasies, and the discrepancy between what the narrator says and what he thinks. His self-created “religion” of precise calm provides a key to the voice. Even when describing abandonment, foreclosure, danger, or resentment, he tends to intellectualise, joke, or narrativise his experience. Short admissions such as “My father: gone for months” and “I felt strong. He noticed me. I felt headless” puncture the more expansive passages with compressed emotional force.

The structure is braided and nonlinear, alternating among the narrator’s present life at the home improvement store, memories of his father’s behaviour, and a childhood Anansi tale performed by the father. Transitions often occur without explanation, requiring the reader to infer the thematic relationship between strands. The folktale functions as more than an inset story: Lion’s appetite, arrogance, and impatience echo the father, while Anansi’s resourcefulness reflects the narrator’s need to survive through intelligence, imagination, and self-control. The embedded tale also preserves the father at his most affectionate and creative, complicating any simple judgment of him as merely neglectful. As the story advances, the folktale moves toward Anansi’s victory while the realistic plot moves toward the father’s return, creating parallel forms of suspense with sharply different kinds of resolution.

The prose combines conversational naturalism with sudden lyric compression. Sentences frequently begin plainly and accumulate clauses, qualifications, or imaginative extensions, mimicking the narrator thinking his way around feelings he cannot address directly. These longer passages are counterbalanced by fragments and brief declarative sentences. Colons are used to create abrupt equivalences or revelations, as in “My father: gone for months,” while repetition gives emotional moments a restrained rhythm. The final exchange—“Dad,” followed by the narrator’s inability to say more—uses withheld speech as its central effect. Internal statements such as “There’s food in the fridge because of me” reveal the confrontation that cannot occur aloud.

The diction moves fluidly between colloquial teenage speech, workplace terminology, comic-book and film references, and elevated figurative language. Technical objects—pallet jacks, bolt cutters, nylon vests, forklifts, washing machines, paint cans—give the workplace scenes tactile credibility. At the same time, the narrator recasts ordinary labour through heroic and mythic frameworks: the unload crew becomes “the Specialists,” trailers become villains and caves, and Cato becomes Hercules. This mock-epic register is humorous but also psychologically protective. It grants dignity and adventure to exhausting, low-paid work while exposing how badly the narrator needs an alternative story about his circumstances.

Humour is pervasive but defensive rather than frivolous. It appears in the imagined action-movie roles of the workers, Cato’s repeated “Hercules,” the attractiveness rankings, Reese’s crude encouragement, and the elaborate fantasy of discovering baby Cristie behind the appliances. These comic passages humanise the characters and delay direct confrontation with the narrator’s fear. They also tend to darken as they unfold. The fantasy of finding a baby, for example, begins whimsically but becomes a vision of shared, distant fatherhood, connecting the narrator’s longing for care with his own forced assumption of parental responsibility.

Dialogue is concise, idiomatic, and strongly differentiated by character. The father speaks with authority, impatience, and casual assumptions about obedience; the mother answers pain with composed resignation; Cato’s language is playful and fraternal; Reese mixes vulgarity, prejudice, encouragement, and awkward affection. The Anansi sections use a more performative oral cadence, including repetition, direct address, exclamations, and phrases such as “You will see.” The references to English and Twi, Ghana, Anansi, and the Togo Mountains establish a diasporic cultural background without turning the narration into exposition. Folklore is presented as a living family practice embodied through the father’s voices, hands, and movements.

Characterisation relies heavily on gesture, work habits, and contradiction. The father is both the imaginative storyteller who makes his children “stars” and the man who repeatedly leaves them waiting. The mother’s calm simultaneously comforts, wounds, and teaches the narrator the emotional discipline he later adopts. Cato is both a fallen school “god” and a generous coworker who urges the narrator not to become trapped. Reese is rendered with moral ambiguity: he may be racist, yet he is also dependable, encouraging, and proud of the narrator. Rather than resolving these contradictions, the story allows affection and distrust, admiration and disappointment, to coexist.

Imagery repeatedly centres on mouths, stomachs, weight, containment, and unloading. Lion swallows the rabbit children; trucks have “guts” and “mouths”; trailers hold tightly packed objects; washing machines pin Cato down; anguish sits like lead in the narrator’s stomach. These motifs connect consumption and physical burden to familial and economic pressure. The unloading job becomes an extended metaphor for the narrator’s emotional condition: he digs through packed, dangerous interiors hoping to find something meaningful at the end, only to reach “a tall slab of nothing.” Hands are similarly important. The father’s hands become Lion and Anansi, workers handle dangerous loads, and the father’s returning hand rests on the narrator’s shoulder in a gesture that is affectionate but inadequate.

Pacing alternates between summary and vivid scene. Months of labour or abandonment may be compressed into a sentence, while accidents, remembered humiliations, and moments with the father are slowed into concrete action and dialogue. The repeated returns to the shipment truck create a cyclical, oppressive rhythm: school, work, sleep, dread, and another truck. Against this repetition, the father’s return arrives suddenly and almost anticlimactically, in a paint aisle on a day when there is no truck. The ordinary setting prevents cathartic melodrama and keeps the emotional emphasis on the narrator’s paralysis.

The dominant themes are abandonment, premature adulthood, economic precarity, masculinity, storytelling, and the unstable boundary between care and harm. Fatherhood appears in multiple forms: biological, failed, imagined, fraternal, and improvised. The narrator tries to parent his sister, imagines the workers becoming secret fathers to an abandoned baby, regards Cato as a brother, and receives from Reese the affirmation his own father has not provided. The story also examines survival through narrative. The father uses folklore to enchant his children; the narrator uses movies, superheroes, jokes, and fantasies to make labour and fear bearable. Yet these invented frameworks do not erase reality, and the story repeatedly exposes the emptiness behind them.

The ending is deliberately unresolved and emotionally ambivalent. The narrator has imagined his father gone forever and has proved his own competence, but the father’s return instantly destabilises that hard-won identity. His thoughts contain accusation, pride, gratitude, and bewilderment, while his spoken responses remain minimal and compliant. The final “Yes, I do” answers the practical question of whether he needs a ride, but it also captures his continuing dependence on the person who abandoned him. The style avoids explicit reconciliation or condemnation, closing instead on the tension between injury and attachment.

generation.response_text:
The truck was supposed to arrive at four, which meant it came at five-thirty, after we had spent ninety minutes preparing ourselves spiritually for disaster.

My religion at seventeen was Precise Calm. It had one commandment: do not let anybody see the exact size of the thing sitting on your chest.

Precise Calm allowed you to say, “No problem,” when the electric company sent a red envelope. It allowed you to make macaroni for your little sister and call it Italian Night. It allowed you to stand behind the home improvement store in a reflective orange vest, watching rain turn the loading dock black, while your mother’s medicine waited at the pharmacy and your father had been in Ghana for fourteen weeks.

He had said two.

“Trailer’s here,” Reese announced.

He was smoking under the NO SMOKING sign. Reese believed signs were advice from people who had not met him.

Cato rolled his shoulders. “Hercules.”

He said this whenever something required lifting, enduring, or lying to yourself.

“Hercules,” I agreed.

The three of us were the evening unload crew, also known as the Specialists, though only to ourselves. Cato was Weapons and Heavy Artillery. Reese was Intelligence, because he was forty-six and knew which managers were sleeping together. I was Reconnaissance, because I was skinny enough to climb over the merchandise and report what was trying to kill us.

The trailer backed toward the dock with the shrill beeping of a hospital machine. Its rear doors opened. Inside were refrigerators, grills, toilets, lawn mowers, boxed cabinets, and several hundred cartons positioned according to a system invented by men who hated gravity.

Cato peered into the darkness.

“Behold,” he said. “The beast.”

The trailer’s mouth stood open. Its silver guts waited.

We went in.

* * *

When my father told stories, his hands stopped belonging to him.

His right hand became Anansi: small, twitchy, quick, the fingers bent into legs. His left hand became whichever fool had chosen that night to underestimate Anansi. Often it was Lion.

Lion had my father’s deep voice, enlarged. Lion was all stomach and command.

“Bring me food,” Lion would roar, and my little sister, Abena, would scream happily even though she knew Lion was coming. She always knew. Knowing never saved her from delight.

Anansi spoke fast, sometimes in English, sometimes in Twi, sometimes in a language my father claimed was spoken only by spiders and troublesome children.

One night Lion found three rabbit children playing beneath a silk-cotton tree.

“Three?” I asked.

“Three,” my father said.

“Why didn’t their mother watch them?”

My father frowned at me. I was ten and already irritating stories with logistics.

“The mother had gone to gather cassava.”

“She left all three?”

“You want me to tell it, or you want to tell it?”

Abena slapped my arm. “Let Daddy tell.”

My father’s left hand opened wide. Lion’s mouth.

The rabbit children ran. Lion was faster. One, two, three: he swallowed them whole.

Abena gasped.

My father smiled because he had made the world dangerous, and because only he knew how to make it safe again.

* * *

The first thing inside the trailer was a tower of paint cans leaning toward Cato.

I said, “Left.”

He moved right.

“Your other left.”

The cans trembled. Cato put both palms against them and held.

“Hercules,” he whispered.

Cato had run the two hundred meters in twenty-one-point-something when he was a junior. His picture still lived in the trophy case at our school, although he himself had graduated three years before and now lived mainly in receiving. In the photograph, he was crossing a finish line with his mouth open, all tendon and triumph. At work he wore a black brace around his left knee and moved carefully until something began to fall. Then his body remembered being fast.

I slid the pallet jack under the paint. Reese guided the forks.

“Easy, Professor,” he told me.

He called me Professor because I had been accepted to colleges, a fact he repeated more faithfully than I did.

The pallet shifted. Three cans rolled loose. Cato caught one against his chest, trapped one with his boot, and let the third fall.

It hit the trailer floor without bursting.

We stared at it.

“That,” Reese said, “is why the Lord invented underpaid youth.”

My religion had no official relationship with the Lord, but I accepted the miracle.

We dragged the pallet out. Rain misted through the dock opening and cooled the sweat on my neck. My phone buzzed in my pocket. I hoped it was my father, then hated myself for hoping, then hoped harder.

It was Abena.

MOM SAYS GET MILK.

A second message arrived.

AND NOT THE WEIRD KIND.

The weird kind was powdered.

I wrote: OK.

There was food in our refrigerator because of me. Milk, when available, was also because of me. This thought sometimes made me stand taller. Sometimes it made me want to lie down in traffic.

Precise Calm had no position on which.

* * *

My father left on a Sunday morning in February.

He wore a blue shirt and the cologne my mother liked, the one that entered a room before he did and remained after he left. His suitcase stood by the door. It was the large brown one, which worried me. A two-week trip should not require a suitcase that could hold a smaller person.

“Your grandmother has business with the land,” he said.

“What land?”

“Our land.”

We had never visited this land. It appeared in conversations the way kingdoms appear in fairy tales: vast, disputed, requiring money.

My mother sat at the kitchen table with both hands around a mug. Her wrists looked too thin. The treatment made her nauseous in the mornings and tired in the afternoons, but she still dressed for work three days a week at the daycare, where other people paid her to watch their children.

“Two weeks,” my father said.

He said it to all of us, but he looked at me.

“Help your mother.”

I was eating cereal. The spoon stopped halfway to my mouth.

It is possible to receive an order and an abandonment in the same sentence.

“Okay,” I said.

He squeezed Abena until she complained, kissed my mother’s forehead, and put a hand on the back of my neck. He did not hug me. We had reached the age when fathers and sons exchanged brief, coded pressures, as if affection were information that might be intercepted.

“You are the man here,” he said.

My mother’s eyes moved toward him. Only for a second.

He took the suitcase outside.

Two weeks later, my mother made jollof because he was coming home. She seasoned the chicken and told Abena to clean the living room. I kept checking the street through the blinds.

At eleven, my mother put the food away.

“He missed his connection,” she said.

She said it calmly. Calm was her inheritance to me.

The next morning, his phone went straight to voicemail.

* * *

Lion slept after his meal, his belly round beneath the silk-cotton tree.

Inside him, the three rabbit children cried.

“Can’t they just climb out?” Abena asked.

“Through where?” I said.

She considered this and hid her face in a cushion.

Anansi came walking along. My father’s fingers traveled over his knee, light and quick.

He heard the rabbit children singing from Lion’s stomach:

Anansi, Anansi, clever and small,  
Lion has eaten us, fur, feet and all.

“That doesn’t rhyme,” I said.

“It rhymes in Twi.”

“You said it in English.”

My father gave me a look. In that look I was not merely wrong; I was exhausting centuries.

Anansi climbed onto Lion’s nose and shouted, “Wake up, great king!”

Lion opened one eye.

“Who disturbs me?”

“Only your servant, who has come to warn you.”

“Warn me of what?”

“A terrible sickness. It begins with the swallowing of rabbits.”

Lion sat up.

My father sat up, too. Abena clutched my arm. His stories used our bodies as furniture.

“I have swallowed no rabbits,” Lion said.

From his stomach came three small voices: “Liar!”

Lion slapped both paws over his belly.

Anansi pretended not to hear.

* * *

By April, the mortgage company had called enough times that I recognized the number.

My mother stopped answering. I started.

I became a courteous middle-aged man on the telephone.

“Yes, I understand.”

“No, sir, she is not available.”

“Yes, we are aware of the amount.”

“When can you expect payment?” the man asked.

Behind me, Abena was trying to microwave a fork.

“Soon,” I said.

Soon was a useful word. My father had gone to Ghana soon ago. He would return soon. We would pay soon. My mother would feel better soon. Soon had no legal definition and required no down payment.

I hung up and confiscated the fork.

“You can’t put metal in there.”

“I wasn’t going to turn it on.”

“Then why put it in?”

She shrugged. At twelve, Abena regarded causes and consequences as unfriendly rumors.

There had been one call from my father, nine days after he was supposed to return. The connection crackled as if he were speaking from inside a frying pan.

“The matter is complicated,” he said.

“What matter?”

“The land. There are documents.”

Mom was asleep on the couch, one arm over her eyes.

“When are you coming back?”

“Soon.”

“We need—”

The line broke.

I waited for him to call again. He did not.

After that came a message saying his phone had been stolen. Then an email from an address I did not recognize: I am handling things. Be patient. Tell your mother not to worry.

I did not tell her that part. My mother was already performing not worrying full-time.

At school, acceptance letters arrived.

The state university gave me a blue folder with a photograph of students lying on grass, as if college were an organized program of outdoor reclining. A private college two hours away offered aid but not enough. Another school offered enough but was six hours away, which made the amount seem like an accusation.

My guidance counselor called me into her office.

“You haven’t deposited anywhere.”

“I’m comparing packages.”

“The deadline is Friday.”

“I like to be thorough.”

Precise Calm sounded a lot like intelligence if you wore a collared shirt.

She pushed her glasses up. “Is something happening at home?”

“No.”

A small word. Strong enough to hold up a roof, if nobody touched it.

* * *

Cato got pinned by a washing machine on a Thursday.

It happened near the back of the trailer. We had unloaded vanities, lumber, garden chemicals, and a mountain of ceiling fans. The deeper we went, the hotter it became. The trailer smelled of cardboard, dust, metal, and the trapped breath of factories.

The washing machines were stacked two high.

“Bad geometry,” I said.

Reese wiped his face with his vest. “Everything in this building is bad geometry.”

We loosened the straps. The top machine shifted.

There are moments when an object becomes an animal. You see intention in its movement. That washing machine wanted Cato.

He shoved me backward.

The machine tipped, struck his shoulder, and drove him against the wall. His knee folded.

He made a sound I had never heard from him.

Reese and I pushed. The machine weighed more than the combined value of our lives according to payroll, but we moved it enough for Cato to slide free.

He sat on the trailer floor, breathing through his teeth.

“You good?” I asked.

It was a stupid question, but workplaces provide only three responses to injury: You good? Walk it off. Don’t tell management.

Cato looked at his knee.

“Hercules,” he said faintly.

The manager wanted him to finish the shift after ice.

Reese became very still.

Now, Reese had said things about immigrants, women, vegetarians, people from California, people who drove electric cars, and one particular Polish family who had purchased the wrong mulch. Morally, he was a house where several rooms had caught fire. But when the manager suggested Cato could return to work, Reese stepped close enough that the manager looked at his shoes.

“He’s going to urgent care,” Reese said.

“We’re short tonight.”

“You can be shorter.”

Reese drove him.

I stayed because I needed the hours.

For the rest of the shift, I unloaded alone with a temporary worker named Kyle who kept disappearing to vape. I moved toilets and doors. I dragged a pallet of tile that resisted like an anchor. By closing, my arms shook.

At the bus stop, I imagined the washing machine falling on me instead. I imagined not moving fast enough. I imagined my mother getting a call and having to choose whether to wake Abena before going to the hospital.

Then I imagined finding a baby behind a row of refrigerators.

This was a regular fantasy.

The baby’s name was Cristie, because that was printed on a torn shipping label I had once found inside a trailer. She would be wrapped in bubble plastic, unharmed and cheerful. The Specialists would raise her in secret. Cato would teach her to run correctly, once his knee healed. Reese would teach her every word she was not allowed to say at school. I would read to her in the break room and explain algebra.

We would keep diapers behind the insulation and formula in the manager’s refrigerator. During overnight inventory, Cristie would sleep in a display crib in Seasonal. Customers would wonder why three exhausted men kept buying tiny socks.

In later versions of the fantasy, we took turns bringing her home. She learned to call all of us Dad.

This was funny until it wasn’t.

The bus came. I climbed aboard and paid with money I had earned carrying machines that could crush me. Heroic music did not play.

* * *

Lion narrowed his eyes at Anansi.

“What sickness?”

“A royal sickness,” Anansi said. “Too grand for goats. Too powerful for antelope. It afflicts only kings who swallow three rabbit children before sunset.”

Lion’s ears flattened.

“What is the cure?”

Anansi paced across my father’s arm.

“The cure is difficult.”

“I am Lion. Nothing is difficult.”

“You must open your mouth.”

Lion opened it.

“Wider.”

Lion opened wider.

“Wider still.”

My father opened his own mouth so wide Abena squealed. His gold tooth flashed. He had broken the original tooth playing football when he was young, though he claimed different opponents depending on the audience: a boy from Accra, a soldier, a goat.

Anansi peered into Lion’s throat.

“Very serious,” he said. “I see rabbit fever.”

The three children shouted from below, “We are not fever!”

“Hush,” Anansi whispered. “Do you want saving or do you want accuracy?”

I laughed hardest at that line. My father noticed.

Being noticed by him was like having sunlight choose you.

* * *

Cato returned three days later with a new brace and doctor’s orders forbidding lifting.

The manager assigned him to inventory, which meant he walked around with a scanner and lied about not lifting.

We ate lunch on overturned buckets behind Receiving. Reese had a meatball sub. Cato had chips. I had crackers from the vending machine because I had used lunch money for milk.

Cato pointed at my crackers. “That’s not food.”

“It has a nutrition label.”

“So does dog food.”

“Luxury dog food is expensive.”

Reese chewed and looked at me. “You decide on college?”

“Working on it.”

“Work faster.”

“I may take a year.”

Cato stopped eating.

Reese said, “No.”

I laughed. “Thank you, admissions committee.”

“I’m serious.”

“So am I.”

“You got accepted.”

“I also got bills.”

Reese waved one thick hand. “Everybody got bills.”

“Not everybody’s are mine.”

The words came out sharper than Precise Calm permitted.

Cato leaned forward, forearms on his knees. “You take a year, this place eats it. Then another. Soon you’re thirty and arguing with Gary about overtime.”

From inside the building came the beep of a forklift reversing.

“I’m not staying forever.”

“I said that,” Cato replied.

He did not sound tragic. That made it worse.

Reese wrapped the rest of his sandwich and shoved it toward me.

“I don’t want that.”

“Didn’t ask.”

He lit a cigarette.

After a while he said, “Your old man still overseas?”

“Yes.”

“When’s he back?”

“Soon.”

Reese blew smoke toward the dumpsters. “Right.”

That right contained everything I did not let people say.

I ate the sandwich.

* * *

My father had disappeared before, but only in smaller units.

An evening. A weekend. Once, five days.

He would come home carrying explanations and sometimes gifts. A wooden bracelet for Mom. A football jersey for me. A doll for Abena whose eyelids did not close at the same time.

My mother never shouted when he returned. Her calm was more frightening than shouting. She would stand at the sink while he spoke about helping a friend or fixing a problem or needing space to think.

“Space,” she once said, washing the same plate for several minutes. “You have found much of it.”

Later he took us for ice cream. He let Abena order two scoops and told an Anansi story in the car. By the time we came home, we were laughing. My mother was not.

I used to think this meant she did not understand forgiveness.

Now I understood she was tired of being made into an audience.

Still, my father could cook eggs with peppers the exact way I liked them. He attended every one of my middle-school award ceremonies and whistled when my name was called. He taught me to change a tire, to greet elders properly, to never allow someone to insult Ghanaian football in my presence unless I knew how many people were with them.

He made Abena and me stars in his stories.

We were hunters, queens, children born carrying golden drums. We crossed the Togo Mountains in one night. We answered riddles that defeated chiefs. Whenever danger came, he leaned close and asked, “And who can save them now?”

We shouted our own names.

This was the trouble. He had taught us to expect rescue in his voice.

* * *

At the end of April, my mother fainted in the kitchen.

She did not fall dramatically. She placed one hand on the counter, missed the chair, and folded down as if obeying careful instructions.

Abena screamed.

I called the ambulance. I found Mom’s insurance card. I packed her medications in a plastic grocery bag. In the emergency room, I answered questions while Abena sat with her knees tucked beneath her chin.

“Spouse?” the nurse asked.

“Out of the country.”

“Can he be reached?”

“No.”

My mother opened her eyes.

“He is in Ghana,” she whispered, as if clarifying made it respectable.

They kept her overnight for dehydration and adjusted two prescriptions. The copay erased most of that week’s paycheck.

On the bus home the next morning, Abena slept against my shoulder. Her hair smelled like hospital air and coconut oil. I looked at our reflections in the window: one child pretending to be unconscious, one pretending not to be a child.

At home, the mailbox held a foreclosure warning.

I put it beneath my mattress.

There was food in the fridge because of me.

My mother was home because I had called.

My sister was safe because I had watched her.

My father: elsewhere.

I felt powerful. I felt robbed. Mostly I needed sleep.

* * *

Anansi asked Lion to lie on his back.

“To cure rabbit fever,” he said, “you must remain completely still.”

Lion lay down.

“Now I need a vine.”

“What for?”

“To pull out the sickness.”

Anansi tied one end of the vine to a tree. He carried the other end across Lion’s teeth and told him to bite.

“Hard,” Anansi said.

Lion bit.

Anansi pulled the vine tight, forcing Lion’s mouth to remain open.

My father spread his fingers. His left hand became a cage of teeth. His right hand crept toward it.

“Then Anansi entered Lion’s mouth,” he said quietly.

Abena said, “No.”

“Anansi is brave,” my father said.

“Anansi is stupid,” I said.

“Sometimes these are cousins.”

He made Anansi descend past the tongue, down the throat, into the enormous dark of Lion.

Inside Lion’s stomach sat the three rabbit children, wet, frightened, and offended.

“You took long enough,” said the oldest.

“Do you want saving,” Anansi asked, “or do you want to complain?”

“Both,” said the middle one.

“That is reasonable,” Anansi said.

* * *

Graduation was one week away when the truck did not come.

No truck meant we were assigned to the sales floor, a place of unnatural brightness where customers asked questions such as, “Where are your nails?” while standing beneath a sign that said NAILS.

I was straightening paint samples when Reese appeared.

“Professor.”

He jerked his head toward the end of the aisle.

A man stood there in a blue button-down shirt. He was thinner than I remembered, or maybe I had built him larger during his absence. He had more gray in his beard. Beside his shoes sat the brown suitcase.

My father.

For one second my mind rejected him as a badly placed object. He belonged at the airport, at our front door, in an argument with my mother. Not between Interior Satin and Weather-Resistant Exterior.

He smiled.

It was not a big smile. He had enough sense for that.

“Kojo,” he said.

Cato came around the corner carrying a scanner. He saw my face, then saw the man. Cato’s expression changed.

My father walked toward me.

Three and a half months late.

He put his hand on my shoulder.

His hand was warm. Familiar pressure. The old code.

“My son.”

I had prepared speeches.

On buses, in trailers, during chemistry, while lying awake listening to my mother cough, I had addressed him with the disciplined fury of a lawyer in the final scene of a movie. I told him about the mortgage company and the ambulance. I held up pharmacy receipts. I made him look at Abena’s face when the phone rang. I explained what soon meant when rent was due.

In some versions I punched him.

In others I refused to speak.

In the most satisfying version, I walked past him carrying an enormous refrigerator by myself.

Now he stood in front of me, thinner and older, smelling of travel and that same cologne.

“Dad,” I said.

That was all.

His fingers tightened on my shoulder.

“I came directly here,” he said. “Your mother told me you were working.”

Of course he had spoken to her first. The idea hurt and relieved me simultaneously.

“You have grown,” he said.

I had not. Not in inches.

Behind him, Reese pretended to study caulk. Cato did not pretend anything.

My father looked at my vest, my work gloves, the dust on my pants. Pride entered his face as if he had discovered something he had planted.

“You are helping the family.”

There was food in the refrigerator because of me.

Mom’s prescriptions were paid because of me.

Abena’s field-trip form had twenty dollars clipped to it because of me.

I wanted to tell him he did not get to be proud. I wanted him to be proud. I wanted him to apologize in the paint aisle until the store closed and the lights went out and we were left among the gallons of color with nowhere to hide.

Instead I said, “Yeah.”

His hand remained on my shoulder. Affectionate. Insufficient.

* * *

Anansi could not lead the rabbit children back through Lion’s throat because the passage was too narrow.

“What will they do?” Abena asked.

“You will see,” my father said.

Anansi searched Lion’s stomach. There he found everything Lion had swallowed without thinking: bones, bells, half a drum, a hunter’s sandal, two cooking pots, a spearhead, seven stones, and a gourd filled with palm oil that somehow had not spilled.

“Why not?” I asked.

“Magic gourd.”

“Convenient.”

“All magic is convenient.”

Anansi poured the oil along the walls of Lion’s stomach until everything became slick.

Then he instructed the rabbit children to climb into one cooking pot. Anansi climbed into the other.

“Now,” he shouted, “we make Lion angry.”

They banged the pots against Lion’s ribs.

Boom. Boom. Boom.

My father drummed his fists against his chest.

Lion roared. The vine held his jaws open. The rabbits banged harder. Anansi jabbed the inside of Lion’s stomach with the spearhead.

Lion coughed.

The first pot shot upward and out of his mouth, carrying the three rabbit children into the grass.

Lion coughed again.

Anansi flew out in the second pot and struck the silk-cotton tree.

Lion snapped the vine and leaped to his feet.

“Anansi!”

But Anansi had climbed high into the branches. The rabbit children were already running home.

“You have cheated me!” Lion shouted.

“No,” Anansi called down. “Your appetite cheated you. I only introduced you.”

My father loved that ending. His teeth showed. His hands returned to being hands.

“And Lion?” Abena asked.

“Lion went hungry.”

“What about the rabbits?”

“They reached their mother.”

“Did she punish them?”

“First she held them,” my father said. “Then she punished them.”

I asked, “What happened to Anansi?”

My father leaned back on the couch.

“Anansi went home.”

* * *

At the store, my father glanced toward Reese and Cato.

“These are your friends?”

“Coworkers.”

Cato stepped forward first. He held out his hand.

“Cato.”

My father shook it.

“Thank you for looking after my son.”

Cato looked at me, then back at him. “He looks after us.”

Reese came next, wiping his palm on his jeans before offering it.

“Reese.”

“Pleasure.”

Reese nodded once. His face revealed nothing. For perhaps the first time in his life, he kept every opinion indoors.

My father said, “I have heard he will attend university.”

The aisle seemed to narrow.

“I’ve been accepted,” I said.

“You will go,” my father replied.

He said it with his old authority, as if my future had been waiting for his signature. Anger moved through me, clean and hot. Also gratitude, which was worse.

“How?” I asked.

It was the first true thing I had said.

His eyes shifted. Only slightly.

“We will discuss it at home.”

That meant there were no answers suitable for paint.

A customer entered the aisle, pushing a cart containing one tiny brush. He looked at our group and reversed out.

My father removed his hand from my shoulder. The place where it had rested felt colder.

“There were problems,” he said. “With the family land. Your uncle—”

I nearly laughed. The family land. The mythical kingdom. Acres of complicated soil powerful enough to erase phone calls.

He stopped.

Perhaps my face had spoken.

“I should have called more,” he said.

This was not enough. It was something.

Cato’s scanner beeped. Reese studied the ceiling.

My father looked tired. Not story tired, when he leaned back and asked Abena to bring water. Truly tired. There were hollows beneath his eyes, and one cuff of his shirt had torn. I noticed these details against my will.

Precise Calm instructed me to inventory facts:

He had left.

He had returned.

The bills remained.

I loved him.

I was angry.

No fact canceled another.

My manager appeared at the far end of the aisle. He saw us and made the expression managers make when human life interferes with scheduling.

“You need something?” he called.

“My father,” I said.

The manager waited, perhaps expecting the rest of the sentence.

My father: what?

Back from Ghana. Gone for months. Teller of stories. Owner of land. Eater of time. A man with a torn cuff and an inadequate hand.

“My father is here,” I finished.

The manager looked at the suitcase.

“You can take five.”

Five minutes for resurrection.

We walked toward the garden-center doors. Outside, the rain had stopped, leaving the parking lot washed and shining. My father’s car was parked crookedly near the contractor entrance. Our old car. I had imagined it being repossessed, stolen, abandoned at the airport. There it was.

He picked up the suitcase.

“I brought things for you and Abena,” he said.

I wondered what object could survive the distance between us. A shirt. A book. A wooden spider. An explanation folded small enough to fit between socks.

“You graduate next week,” he said.

“Saturday.”

“I will be there.”

I looked at him.

He understood. His mouth tightened.

“I will be there,” he repeated, quieter.

Through the glass doors, I could see Cato and Reese pretending not to watch. Cato raised one fist near his chest.

Hercules.

My father took out his keys.

“Do you need a ride home?”

The bus would come in forty minutes. If it came. My shift was not over, but Reese would cover me. Cato would tell the manager there had been a family emergency, which was true three months late.

I could have said no.

I could have made him wait. I could have chosen the bus, the long route, the hard plastic seat, the life I had managed without him. For months I had been carrying boxes out of dark places. I had learned weight, leverage, how to brace my feet, how to keep my hands clear when a load began to fall.

But I was tired.

I wanted to see my mother’s face when he walked through the door. I wanted to hear Abena shout. I wanted, against evidence and dignity, the end of the story.

My father opened the passenger door.

“Yes,” I said. “I do.”

## The Lighthouse at the End of the Road

By the time Mara Vale reached the lighthouse, the sea had already forgotten the sun.

She stood beside her motorcycle, one hand on the warm engine, and stared across the salt marsh. A narrow road ran through the reeds toward a tower of black stone. No waves broke around it. No gulls circled its lantern room. The lighthouse rose from the marsh as though the ocean had retreated centuries ago and left it behind.

Her map insisted there was nothing here.

That was why she had come.

Three days earlier, Mara had received a letter at the city archive, where she spent her working hours repairing maps too old to be useful and too beautiful to discard. The envelope bore no stamp. Her name was written across it in blue ink.

Inside was a single sheet of paper.

*Dear Mara,*

*I have found the road your father was looking for.*

*Come before the next new moon. Bring his compass.*

*—Elias Flint*

She had read it six times before checking the date. The next new moon was that night.

Elias Flint had been her father’s closest friend, a cartographer with bright red hair and a talent for offending wealthy patrons. He had disappeared twelve years ago. Most people assumed he had fallen from a cliff or drowned while surveying the northern coast.

Mara had assumed he was dead.

Now, as darkness gathered in the marsh, she took her father’s brass compass from her jacket. Its needle had never pointed north. It wandered without purpose, trembling toward walls, windows, empty chairs. Her father had claimed it was not broken.

“It points to what is missing,” he used to say.

Mara had been nine when he vanished.

The compass needle turned toward the lighthouse.

She left the motorcycle by the reeds and continued on foot.

The road was paved with pale stones. Up close, she saw lines carved into them—coastlines, rivers, tiny mountains. Each stone was a map, but none showed a country she recognized. The marsh whispered on either side of her. There was no wind.

At the lighthouse door, she found an iron knocker shaped like a closed eye.

Before she could lift it, the door opened.

A thin old man stood inside, holding a lantern. His hair was white now, but his eyebrows were still red.

“Mara,” Elias Flint said. “You have Thomas’s eyes.”

“You have his compass?”

“No. I said to bring it.”

“You said you found the road he was looking for.”

Elias glanced over her shoulder, toward the marsh. “Come inside. We have very little night.”

The door closed behind her with a sound like a book being shut.

The lighthouse smelled of dust, lamp oil, and rain. Shelves covered the curved walls. They were crowded with rolled charts, glass bottles, measuring instruments, and objects Mara could not name. A wooden staircase spiraled upward around a hollow central shaft.

A round table stood in the middle of the room. On it lay a map beneath a sheet of glass.

Mara approached.

The map showed the city where she lived: its bridges, canals, railway stations, and crowded southern districts. Yet the city on the paper was incomplete. Streets ended abruptly. Whole neighborhoods were pale, as if erased. The river divided into seven branches instead of three. At its northern edge, a road curved out beyond the city wall and continued into blank parchment.

Mara leaned closer.

“This is wrong.”

“Not wrong,” Elias said. “Unfinished.”

“Who drew it?”

“Your father.”

The room seemed to tilt. Mara gripped the table.

“My father mapped the eastern islands. He was working there when his ship disappeared.”

“That is what I told everyone.”

“What happened?”

Elias set his lantern beside the map. Its flame burned blue.

“Thomas discovered that maps do not simply describe the world. The oldest maps—the true ones—also persuade it. Draw a border often enough and people will build a wall. Give a place a name and travelers will begin to find it. Remove a village from every chart, and in time even the roads may forget how to reach it.”

Mara looked toward the shelves.

“You expect me to believe maps are magic?”

“I expect you to remember your childhood.”

She did not answer.

“Your father drew maps for you,” Elias continued. “Kingdoms under the kitchen table. Islands in rain puddles. Doors that appeared only on Tuesdays.”

“Games.”

“Were they?”

A memory surfaced before she could stop it: a tiny red door drawn in chalk on the garden wall. Her father telling her to knock three times. For one impossible second, she had smelled pine trees and snow, though it was midsummer.

She had buried that memory beneath years of sensible explanations.

“What does this have to do with his disappearance?” she asked.

Elias touched the blank portion of the map.

“He found evidence of a lost road. Not a road erased from maps, but one that had never been drawn. It runs between places that have been forgotten.”

“Places don’t get forgotten.”

“Everything gets forgotten.”

He lifted the glass and unrolled a second chart over the first. It was covered in names written in different hands.

*The Room Behind the Nursery.*

*The Orchard of Unsent Letters.*

*Saint Orra, Where It Rains Upward.*

*The Last Station Before Morning.*

Some names were crossed out. Others faded as Mara watched.

“Your father believed the road could lead to anything lost,” Elias said. “A city. A memory. A person.”

Her fingers tightened around the compass.

“You said you found it.”

“I found an entrance. It appears during the new moon, from the first moment of full darkness until dawn. The lighthouse keeps it stable.”

“And my father?”

“I think he entered the road twelve years ago.”

“You think?”

“I watched him go.”

Mara struck him.

The sound cracked through the circular room. Elias staggered against the table but did not lift a hand to defend himself.

“You told my mother he drowned.”

“Yes.”

“She waited for him until she died.”

“I know.”

“You let me believe he was dead.”

“I hoped he was.”

The answer stopped her.

Elias touched his bleeding lip.

“Those who travel the road are changed by it. Some find what they seek. Some find what they fear. Most do not return. Thomas made me promise to destroy his map if he failed to come back.”

“But you didn’t.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because I was a coward. And because he was my friend.”

Above them, something heavy moved in the lantern room.

Elias looked up sharply.

“It is beginning.”

A bell rang within the tower.

Its note was low and enormous. Mara felt it in her ribs. Dust drifted from the shelves. The blue flame stretched toward the ceiling.

The compass needle spun once, then fixed on the hollow shaft at the lighthouse’s center.

Where there had been only darkness, a road now descended.

It hung in empty air, sloping downward beneath the floor. Pale paving stones shone beneath a sky filled with unfamiliar stars. On either side stood black trees with silver leaves.

Mara approached the edge.

“Where does it lead?”

“Tonight?” Elias asked. “That depends on you.”

He handed her the blue lantern.

“No,” she said. “You’re coming.”

His expression hardened.

“I cannot.”

“You owe me the truth.”

“I owe you more than I can repay.”

“Then start walking.”

For a moment, he looked almost amused. Then he took a long coat from a peg and stepped onto the road.

The air changed at once.

The lighthouse vanished behind them, replaced by a stone arch standing alone beneath the stars. Through the arch Mara could still see the round room, but it seemed very far away.

They walked.

The road wound through the silver forest. Mist gathered among the roots, and pale moths followed the lantern. Mara checked the compass every few steps. Its needle pointed ahead.

“What exactly are we looking for?” Elias asked.

“My father.”

“That may not be enough. The road responds to precise desires.”

“I precisely desire to find my father.”

“Do you want the man he was? The man he is now? Do you want an explanation? An apology? A body to bury?”

Mara stopped.

“You knew me when I was a child. Don’t pretend you know me now.”

“I am not pretending anything. The road is dangerous because most people do not know what they truly want.”

“And you do?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

“To undo what I did.”

The silver leaves stirred though there was no breeze.

Mara resumed walking.

After an hour—or perhaps only minutes—the forest ended. They came to a railway platform beneath a bright morning sky. Rain fell upward from the tracks, droplets rising into white clouds.

A station clock had thirteen numbers.

On a bench sat a woman in a yellow dress, reading a newspaper. Mara recognized her mother.

She was young, younger than Mara was now. Her dark hair hung in a braid. Her face was free of the illness that had hollowed it during her final years.

Mara’s breath left her.

“Mum?”

The woman lowered the newspaper and smiled.

“There you are. I’ve been waiting.”

Mara took one step off the road.

Elias caught her arm.

“Let go.”

“That is not your mother.”

The woman folded the paper.

“Mara, darling, don’t listen to him. He always was a liar.”

Her voice was perfect.

Mara remembered that voice singing in the kitchen, whispering stories during thunderstorms, calling her home at dusk. Grief opened like a door inside her.

Her mother held out a hand.

“We can wait for your father together.”

The compass needle pointed down the road, away from the platform.

Mara stared at it.

Then she stepped back.

The station disappeared.

They were standing on the road again, surrounded by a desert of red sand. In the distance, enormous stone figures slept beneath the dunes.

“You could have warned me,” Mara said.

“I did.”

“You could have told me what I would see.”

“I didn’t know.”

“What did you see when you first came here?”

Elias’s face became unreadable.

“A chance to save him.”

Before Mara could ask more, the road split in two.

The left branch climbed toward a city suspended upside down from the clouds. The right descended into a valley where thousands of candles burned.

The compass needle wavered between them.

Elias knelt to examine the paving stones.

“The road is uncertain.”

“About what?”

“You.”

Mara tried to steady her thoughts. She pictured her father as he had been: broad-shouldered, smiling, smelling of ink and tobacco. But the image would not hold. She saw instead the empty chair after he vanished. Her mother standing by the window. The cruel patience of hope.

The needle shifted toward the valley.

They followed.

Each candle rested on a low stone wall. Some were tall and newly lit; others had burned almost to nothing. Names had been carved into the wax.

Mara saw names from history, names of cities destroyed by war, names of extinct birds. One candle bore her mother’s name. Its flame was small but steady.

“What is this place?” she whispered.

“A remembrance,” Elias said. “Or a graveyard.”

Near the valley’s center stood a candle taller than Mara. On its side was written:

*THOMAS VALE.*

Its wick was black. No flame burned.

Mara touched the cold wax.

“He’s dead.”

“Not necessarily.”

“The candle is out.”

“Perhaps it was never lit.”

A laugh came from behind them.

Elias went pale.

A man sat atop the stone wall, turning a silver coin over his knuckles. He had red hair, a red beard, and the narrow face Elias had possessed in old photographs.

Mara looked from the young man to the old one.

“What is this?”

The younger Elias jumped down.

“Took you long enough,” he said.

Old Elias raised both hands. “Mara, stay back.”

“Why? Afraid she’ll learn the rest?” the younger man asked.

“You are not real.”

“Neither is a border, but people die for it.”

The younger Elias smiled at Mara.

“Ask him who drew the false island.”

She turned to the old man.

“What does he mean?”

Elias stared at his younger self.

“Your father and I disagreed,” he said at last. “Thomas wanted the road hidden. I wanted it studied.”

“You wanted to sell it,” the younger man said.

“To governments, queens, generals. Imagine it, Mara. A road to every secret fortress. Every lost treasure. Every enemy’s childhood bedroom.”

“I was foolish,” Elias said.

“You were ambitious,” said his younger self. “Such a cleaner word.”

Mara’s hand closed around the compass.

“The false island,” she prompted.

Elias exhaled.

“I altered Thomas’s map. I added an island where there was none, hoping to redirect the road and prove I understood its rules.”

“But you didn’t,” Mara said.

“No. The island became real.”

A memory returned: reports of a sudden reef in the eastern sea, the wreckage of three ships, the official inquiry that had followed her father’s disappearance.

“His ship struck it,” she said.

“Yes.”

“You killed him.”

“No,” said the younger Elias cheerfully. “Not quite.”

Old Elias lunged at him.

His hands passed through empty air. The younger man broke into red moths, which scattered above the candles.

A voice echoed through the valley.

“Mara!”

She knew it at once.

A figure stood on the road beyond the walls. He wore a weather-stained coat and carried a map case over one shoulder. His hair had gone gray, but he was otherwise as she remembered.

Her father.

Mara could not move.

Thomas Vale smiled uncertainly.

“Little star?”

Only he had called her that.

She ran.

The compass fell from her hand. She crossed the space between them and struck his chest with both fists. He stumbled, and she struck him again.

“You left us!”

“I know.”

“Mum waited for you!”

“I know.”

“She died waiting!”

He caught her wrists, not to restrain her but to hold on.

“I tried to come back.”

“You had twelve years.”

“For you.”

She shook free.

Thomas looked toward Elias, who remained among the candles.

“You brought her here.”

“She deserved the truth,” Elias said.

“She deserved a life untouched by this road.”

“I had one,” Mara said. “It was built around a hole where you should have been.”

Her father closed his eyes.

The valley trembled. Candles toppled. From the darkness beyond the walls came a rustling like millions of turning pages.

“The road doesn’t want us together,” Thomas said. “It gathers the lost. It does not return them easily.”

“Then we leave now.”

“I can’t.”

Mara picked up the compass. Its needle pointed at him.

“You’re what’s missing.”

“No. Look again.”

She looked.

The needle passed over her father. It pointed toward Elias.

The old cartographer stood beside Thomas’s unlit candle, holding the blue lantern.

Understanding came slowly.

“You didn’t send the letter,” Mara said.

Elias shook his head.

Thomas looked at him. “You found a way.”

“A poor one.”

“What did you do?” Mara demanded.

Elias opened the lantern’s small glass door. The flame bent toward his fingers.

“The lighthouse requires a keeper. The road requires balance. Something found, something lost.”

“No,” Thomas said.

Elias smiled faintly. “You always did assume every sacrifice had to be yours.”

He closed his hand over the flame.

The valley vanished in blue fire.

Mara fell onto the stone road. Her father landed beside her. Around them stretched darkness filled with countless doors, windows, archways, and gates. Through each shone a different world.

Elias stood several paces away. Blue light spilled through cracks in his skin.

“I drew the island,” he said. “I broke the road. I let pride turn friendship into ruin. I cannot undo those things, but I can finish the map.”

He took a folded sheet from his coat—the map from the lighthouse—and opened it.

The blank road now ended in a small circle.

Elias placed the paper in the air. It remained there, floating. Then he stepped into the empty circle.

Ink spread around his shoes.

“Stop!” Mara shouted.

She tried to reach him, but the road stretched between them.

Thomas grabbed her hand.

Elias began to fade, becoming lines on parchment: first his boots, then his coat, then the weathered face with its red eyebrows.

“Tell the world I drowned,” he said.

“Absolutely not,” Mara replied.

He laughed once.

Then he was gone.

The map folded itself.

Every door in the darkness slammed shut except one.

Beyond it stood the lighthouse.

Mara and Thomas crossed the threshold as the first edge of dawn appeared over the marsh.

The tower was silent. The shelves were bare. The central shaft contained only darkness. On the table lay a single map, newly drawn.

It showed the lighthouse, the marsh, and the pale road leading west toward the city. In the lower corner, a tiny figure held a lantern.

Thomas touched it with two fingers.

“He waited here all these years?”

Mara studied her father’s face. He had aged, but not enough. The road had stolen twelve years from one of them and given them strangely to the other.

“You don’t get to mourn him yet,” she said.

Thomas lowered his hand.

“No.”

“You’re going to tell me everything.”

“Yes.”

“And then we’re going home.”

He looked toward the door as if the word frightened him.

“Is your mother—”

“Don’t.”

His face folded.

For a moment, Mara wanted to comfort him. For another, she wanted to leave him in the lighthouse and let the marsh swallow the road. Instead, she rolled up the map and placed it under her arm.

Outside, morning had turned the reeds to gold.

Her motorcycle waited where she had left it, silvered with dew. Thomas walked around it suspiciously.

“What happened to your bicycle?”

“Twelve years happened.”

He almost smiled.

Mara handed him the spare helmet. It was too small, but he forced it on.

As she started the engine, the brass compass shifted in her pocket. She drew it out.

For the first time in her life, the needle pointed north.

Then, slowly, it turned toward the lighthouse.

Mara looked back.

The tower was fading in the morning light. Stone became mist; mist became sky. For an instant she saw Elias standing in the lantern room, one hand raised in farewell.

Then the lighthouse disappeared.

Only the road remained, cutting through the marsh toward an empty horizon.

“Where does it go?” Thomas asked.

Mara folded the compass into his hand.

“Not our problem today.”

She climbed onto the motorcycle. After a hesitation, her father sat behind her.

The ride back to the city took four hours. Thomas held the map beneath his coat and asked questions at every turn: about electric cars, glass towers, the price of coffee, the war memorial beside the northern gate. Mara answered some and ignored others.

At noon, they stopped on a hill overlooking the city.

The river shone beneath them. Trains crossed the bridges. Thousands of windows caught the sun.

Thomas removed the helmet.

“I drew this place so many times,” he said. “I was afraid I’d invented it.”

Mara thought of her apartment with its leaking ceiling, the archive full of crumbling charts, and the cemetery where her mother lay beneath a cedar tree. She thought of all the explanations still waiting, all the anger that would not vanish merely because the lost had returned.

“It’s real,” she said. “That doesn’t mean it will be easy.”

“I know.”

“No, you don’t.”

He accepted that.

Below them, the roads of the city branched and crossed, carrying everyone toward something they desired or feared. From a distance, it looked exactly like a map.

Mara started the motorcycle again.

“Which way?” Thomas asked.

She looked at the compass. The needle wandered briefly, searching for what was missing.

Then it pointed home.
